subject: operating-systems
title: Semaphores
summary: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive with an integer count changed by atomic wait and signal operations.

questions.prompt: What does a counting semaphore value commonly represent?
questions.answerKey: A counting semaphore can represent the number of available identical resources or permits.
questions.explanation: A binary semaphore has only two logical availability states.

questions.prompt: What happens when a thread performs wait/P on a semaphore whose count is zero?
options: It blocks or waits until a signal/V makes a permit available
questions.answerKey: Wait consumes a permit or blocks until one is available.
questions.explanation: The decrement and test must be atomic.

questions.prompt: A buffer has capacity 8. Which initial semaphore count represents empty slots?
questions.answerKey: The empty-slot semaphore starts at the buffer capacity, 8.
questions.explanation: A separate full-slot semaphore typically starts at zero.

questions.prompt: Why must semaphore wait and signal operations be atomic?
options: Otherwise concurrent updates can lose permits or admit too many threads
It converts a semaphore into a file
questions.answerKey: Non-atomic updates can race and violate the count invariant.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is about the semaphore operation, not about making the protected work indivisible.

questions.prompt: Describe how two semaphores can coordinate a bounded producer-consumer buffer.
questions.answerKey: Use an empty semaphore initialized to capacity and a full semaphore initialized to zero, plus mutual exclusion for buffer indices. A producer waits on empty, inserts, then signals full; a consumer waits on full, removes, then signals empty.
questions.explanation: Counting semaphores track slots; a mutex or equivalent protects the data structure itself.

questions.prompt: Contrast a binary semaphore with a mutex and identify one reason a mutex may be preferable for ownership.
questions.answerKey: Both can enforce exclusion, but a mutex typically has ownership semantics: the thread that locks it must unlock it, enabling misuse checks and priority-inheritance protocols. A binary semaphore is a signaling primitive and may allow different wait/signal participants depending on the API.
questions.explanation: Exact semantics vary by OS, so avoid claiming every semaphore has identical behavior.
